lesson.title: Powers: Base and Exponent Working Together
lesson.summary: A power is the combined result of a base and an exponent, with squaring and cubing as its two most familiar special cases in geometry.
lesson.body:
A power is the complete expression formed when a base is raised to an exponent, such as 4^3, and it also refers to the numerical value that expression represents, in this case 64. The vocabulary can feel circular at first: 4^3 is called a power, and it is also read aloud as four to the third power or four cubed. What matters is that power refers to the whole package working together, the base 4 and the exponent 3 combined, not just one piece of it.

Certain small powers have special spoken names worth knowing. Raising a number to the exponent 2 is called squaring it, so 7^2 is read seven squared, and it equals 49; this name comes from the area of a square with side length 7. Raising a number to the exponent 3 is called cubing it, so 2^3 is read two cubed, and it equals 8; this name comes from the volume of a cube with side length 2. Beyond exponent 3, powers are usually just read as to the fourth power, to the fifth power, and so on.

Powers of the same base can be compared directly by comparing their exponents, as long as the base is greater than 1: larger exponents produce larger powers. For example, since 2 is a fixed base greater than 1, 2^5 = 32 is larger than 2^3 = 8. But this pattern flips for bases between 0 and 1: larger exponents actually produce smaller powers, since (1/2)^5 = 1/32 is smaller than (1/2)^3 = 1/8. Recognizing which regime you are in avoids a common estimation mistake.

Worked example: a square garden bed has side length 6 feet, and a cube shaped storage bin has edge length 4 feet. Find the area of the garden bed and the volume of the bin. The garden bed's area is a power: 6 squared, or 6^2 = 6 * 6 = 36 square feet. The bin's volume is also a power: 4 cubed, or 4^3 = 4 * 4 * 4 = 64 cubic feet. Both answers come directly from evaluating a power, which is exactly why squaring and cubing show up so often in geometry.

Powers of ten deserve special mention because they underlie place value and scientific notation. 10^2 = 100, 10^3 = 1000, and each additional exponent multiplies the previous result by 10 again, adding one more zero. This pattern makes it easy to estimate the size of a power of ten just by counting the exponent, and it is the same pattern that later lets very large or very small measurements be written compactly using scientific notation, where a number is expressed as a value between 1 and 10 multiplied by a power of ten.

Power builds on both exponent and base, since it is literally the combination of the two: a base tells you what is being repeated, an exponent tells you how many times, and a power is the resulting expression and value together. From here forward, the vocabulary is settled: base, exponent, and power will be used precisely and interchangeably with these meanings as you move into the rules that let you combine, simplify, and manipulate powers, starting with integer exponents next.
